A3

Databases

SL: 11 hours | HL: 18 hours

Summary

In this unit, you learn how structured data is stored, organised and queried. You study relational databases, schema design, entity–relationship diagrams, keys, referential integrity, normalization, SQL, transactions, views, and, at HL, alternative databases and data warehouses.

Objectives

You will learn:

  • what makes a relational database useful and where its limits are
  • how databases are modelled and designed
  • how keys, relationships and integrity rules work
  • how normalization improves database structure
  • how SQL is used to define, query and update data
  • at HL, how non-relational models, data warehouses, data mining and distributed databases work

Outcomes

By the end of this unit, you should be able to:

  • explain the features, benefits and limitations of relational databases
  • construct ER diagrams and apply key design principles
  • explain referential integrity and normalization
  • outline DDL and DML
  • construct SQL queries and calculations
  • describe views, transactions and data-warehouse concepts
  • compare relational and non-relational databases

Subtopics

You cover:

  • A3.1 Database fundamentals — relational structure, advantages and limitations
  • A3.2 Database design — schemas, ERDs, data types, keys, referential integrity, normalization and denormalization
  • A3.3 Database programming — SQL language types, joins, filtering, updates, aggregates, views and transactions
  • A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only) — non-relational models, warehouses, mining and distributed systems
